title: What does the future of education LOOK like?
author: Stefan Bauschard
summary: Bauschard uses ChatGPT-4's DALL-E 3 integration as a probe of how machines imagine the future of schooling, recording his own reading of ten generated images before comparing them with the expanded prompts the model silently wrote. He notices that nearly every scene replicates the existing grammar of schooling (lectures, classrooms, a sage on the stage) while removing the human teacher. His central concern is a feedback loop: because writers imagine future education without teachers, the image generators learn and reinforce that picture, and we may be writing and drawing ourselves out of the future. He also observes that the models insert diversity language automatically, likely through RLHF. The piece closes with discussion questions for classroom use. It is exploratory rather than rigorous, but its argument about AI-mediated imagination of schooling is clear.
points: Across ten generated images, the model reproduced lectures, classrooms and sage-on-the-stage structures, merely swapping in robots or holograms.
No image included a human teacher, which the author attributes to the way people writing about future education already imagine it.
He warns of a feedback loop in which imagery and writing about teacher-free futures bake that expectation into the culture.
The model added diversity language to seven of ten prompts, which he guesses reflects RLHF rather than learning from human history.
The exercise is offered as a classroom activity for questioning whether the corpus of past representations binds our thinking about future schooling.
quotes: In this picture, I see a very traditional classroom that simply replicates the existing grammar of education: the “sage” on the stage. The only difference is that the human sage is swapped out for either an AI or a hologram of an individual.
I also don’t think the boy is “Middle Eastern” and the girl is “Hispanic,” but perhaps those thoughts rely on my own stereotypes, which shows how complicated those questions can be.

In no instance did ChatGPT4/Dalle-E3 include a human teacher. I don’t think it deliberately chose to exclude human teachers using RLHF. I think it is because those of us who are writing about the future of education and imagining it are imagining it without human teachers.

If we keep doing this, it is going to bake this into the images of the future, and we will, perhaps, create this world as more and more people come to understand the world this way or expect it to be this way.
Simply put, we may be writing and drawing ourselves out of the future, using AI to replace us as we go.
It is interesting that we’ve mostly replicated the existing “grammars” of schooling while entirely eliminating the human teacher. Hurray! We’ve created the worst of both worlds.
Does relying on image generators that build on the corpus of existing and common representations inherently bind our thinking about the future to the grammars of the past (lectures)?
